title: Agile & Engineering Process
tagline: The Agile Manifesto, Scrum, Kanban, sprints, CI, and code review culture — the human and process side of shipping great software.

sections.content:
Writing good code is necessary but not sufficient. Software is built by **teams**, and teams need process to coordinate, communicate, and deliver value reliably without stepping on each other's work or losing track of what customers actually need. For decades, the dominant model was **waterfall** — define everything upfront, design in full, build in full, test in full, release. It worked for building bridges. It failed spectacularly for software, because software requirements change constantly as customers see working product for the first time and realise what they actually wanted.

In 2001, seventeen software practitioners gathered at a ski lodge in Snowbird, Utah, frustrated with heavyweight processes. They wrote the **Agile Manifesto** — four value statements and twelve principles that have since reshaped how the industry builds software. Agile is not a methodology; it is a **philosophy** — a set of shared beliefs about what matters most when building software under conditions of uncertainty.

**Scrum** and **Kanban** are two frameworks that operationalise Agile values in concrete, day-to-day practices. **Continuous Integration (CI)** is the technical discipline that makes frequent delivery safe. **Code review culture** is the social practice that distributes knowledge and maintains quality across a team. Together, these practices form the backbone of how most professional software teams operate today — and understanding them makes you not just a better individual contributor, but a better teammate.

This chapter covers: the Agile Manifesto and why it was written, Scrum's roles and ceremonies in depth, Kanban's flow model and WIP limits, the mechanics of CI pipelines, best practices for code review, and how these practices interact to create high-performing engineering teams.

sections.title: A Ship That Adjusts Course vs. A Train on Fixed Rails
sections.content:
Traditional waterfall development is like a trans-continental train: the entire route is planned before departure, every stop is scheduled months ahead, and changing direction means halting, reversing, and laying new rails — expensive, slow, and disruptive. The software industry spent decades learning that this metaphor is wrong. Requirements change. Competitors move. Customers discover what they actually want only after seeing a working product. The destination shifts while you are still building the vehicle.

**Agile is a ship**: you have a general direction (product vision), you make short voyages (sprints or flow cycles), you check your instruments at each port of call (retrospectives, reviews), and you adjust the heading before the next leg. The course is never fixed for more than a few weeks. This does not mean chaos — ships have engines, navigators, first officers, and charts. **Scrum** is the navigation protocol: who decides the route, how the crew holds daily briefings, how they debrief after each leg. **Kanban** is the instrument panel: a live display of how work is flowing through the ship, where the queues are building up, and which station is the bottleneck. **CI** is the engine room alarm system — it alerts the whole crew the instant something breaks, before it becomes a catastrophic failure mid-ocean. **Code review** is the second officer, the navigator's check: a trusted second pair of eyes before any significant course change is committed.

The ship metaphor also captures an important nuance: the crew does not change with every voyage. The **team is a stable unit** that improves its navigation skills over repeated trips. Agile works not because of the ceremonies, but because stable, trusted teams that reflect and improve outperform reshuffled groups following heavyweight plans.

sections.title: The Agile Manifesto: Four Values and Twelve Principles
sections.content:
The **Agile Manifesto** opens with a single sentence of humility: 'We are uncovering better ways of developing software by doing it and helping others do it.' The four value statements that follow each compare two things — the left side is valued *more*, but the right side is not discarded:

1. **Individuals and interactions** over processes and tools
2. **Working software** over comprehensive documentation
3. **Customer collaboration** over contract negotiation
4. **Responding to change** over following a plan

Each value statement was a direct reaction to pathologies the authors had witnessed. 'Processes over people' was the world of CMM (Capability Maturity Model) bureaucracy. 'Documentation over software' described projects that produced mountains of specs but no running code. 'Contract negotiation' described the adversarial relationship between IT vendors and clients. 'Following the plan' described teams that knew the plan was wrong but kept executing it anyway because the plan was the contract.

The **twelve principles** expand on these values. The most technically significant: *deliver working software frequently — from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference for the shorter timescale.* This is the principle that drives CI and short sprints. Another important one: *at regular intervals, the team reflects on how to become more effective, then tunes and adjusts its behaviour accordingly* — this is the retrospective. And: *continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility.* Agile is not an excuse for sloppy code; quality is how you keep delivery fast.

A critical misconception to dispel: **Agile does not mean no planning.** It means planning at the right level of detail for the right time horizon. You can plan a quarter at a rough level (roadmap) and a two-week sprint in fine detail. What you cannot do is plan a year in fine detail, because the details will be wrong and the plan will be a fiction that everyone pretends is real.

sections.title: Scrum: Roles, Events, and Artefacts in Depth
sections.content:
Scrum is the most widely adopted Agile framework. It provides concrete answers to: who does what, how often does the team synchronise, and what artefacts make the work visible. It is deliberately lightweight — the entire Scrum Guide is under 20 pages.

**Three Roles:**

- **Product Owner (PO)**: The single person accountable for maximising the value of the product. The PO owns the **Product Backlog** — the ordered list of everything the team might ever build. 'Ordered', not 'prioritised' — the PO decides which item is most valuable *right now*, and that order can change between sprints. The PO is the interface between the business (stakeholders, customers) and the development team. Critically, there is only one PO — multiple stakeholders give input, but one person makes the call.

- **Scrum Master (SM)**: A servant-leader who helps the team follow Scrum, removes impediments, facilitates ceremonies, and protects the team from external interruptions during a sprint. The SM does not assign tasks — that is antithetical to self-organisation. They are also not a project manager; they do not own the plan. Their job is to make the team maximally effective at doing its own work.

- **Developers** (historically 'Development Team'): The self-organising, cross-functional group that turns backlog items into working increments. 'Cross-functional' means the team contains all the skills needed (frontend, backend, QA, design) — they do not depend on external teams to complete a story. 'Self-organising' means the team decides *how* to do the work; nobody assigns tasks from outside.

**Five Events:**

- **Sprint**: A time-box of 1–4 weeks (typically 2 weeks). A Sprint is a mini-project: it starts with a Sprint Goal, ends with a potentially shippable Increment, and is never extended. The time-box creates urgency and a natural cadence for planning and reflection.

- **Sprint Planning**: The team selects items from the top of the Product Backlog and creates a Sprint Backlog — the set of work they commit to completing in the sprint. The PO explains the goal; the team forecasts how much they can do based on their velocity (story points completed per sprint over recent history). The team also defines the **Definition of Done** — what 'complete' means (code reviewed, tested, deployed to staging, docs updated).

- **Daily Scrum (Standup)**: A 15-minute daily synchronisation, same time and place. Three questions: What did I do yesterday that helped achieve the Sprint Goal? What will I do today? Do I have any blockers? The standup is for the developers to coordinate with each other — not a status report to the Scrum Master or managers. Blockers surfaced here are the SM's job to remove.

- **Sprint Review**: At the end of the sprint, the team demonstrates the working Increment to stakeholders. Stakeholders give feedback. The PO updates the backlog based on what they learn. This is where **customer collaboration over contract negotiation** becomes concrete — the plan adapts based on what customers actually see and respond to.

- **Sprint Retrospective**: An internal team meeting (no stakeholders) to reflect on the *process*, not the *product*. The team discusses: what went well, what to improve, and commits to one concrete action. The retrospective is how teams compound improvements — each sprint a little better than the last.

**Three Artefacts:**

- **Product Backlog**: The single source of truth for what the team might build — user stories, bugs, technical debt, research tasks. The PO maintains its order.
- **Sprint Backlog**: The items selected for this sprint plus the plan for delivering them. Owned by the developers.
- **Increment**: The sum of all completed Sprint Backlog items, meeting the Definition of Done. Every Sprint must produce an Increment, even if it is not released to production.

sections.label: Concept
sections.code:
## Sprint 14 — Checkout Payment Flow

### Sprint Goal
By end of Sprint 14, customers can complete checkout with a
saved payment method (Stripe tokenisation).

### Sprint Backlog (selected from Product Backlog)
| ID    | Story                                        | Points | Status      |
|-------|----------------------------------------------|--------|-------------|
| US-41 | User can save a card during checkout         | 5      | In Progress |
| US-42 | User can select a saved card at checkout     | 3      | To Do       |
| US-43 | Card tokenisation via Stripe                 | 8      | To Do       |
| BUG-7 | Checkout fails on mobile Safari              | 2      | Done        |

### Daily Standup — Sarah (Day 3)
**Done yesterday:** Implemented card-save API endpoint; unit tests passing.
**Doing today:**  Integrating Stripe tokenisation; writing integration tests.
**Blockers:**  Need Stripe test API keys from DevOps — @james can you action this?

### Definition of Done (team agreement)
- [ ] Code reviewed by at least one peer
- [ ] All existing tests pass in CI
- [ ] New behaviour covered by unit + integration tests
- [ ] Feature deployed to staging environment
- [ ] PO has accepted the story against acceptance criteria

### Retrospective Actions (carried from Sprint 13)
- [x] Add lint step to CI to catch style issues before review (done, saved ~30 min/PR)
- [ ] Run mob programming session on complex domain logic (scheduled for Sprint 14 day 5)
sections.explanation: A real Sprint Backlog links every story to the Sprint Goal — 'done' is defined at the goal level, not just task-by-task. The Definition of Done is agreed by the whole team and is non-negotiable. Retrospective actions carry forward with explicit owners and completion tracking — otherwise they evaporate between sprints.

sections.title: Kanban: Flow, Visualisation, and WIP Limits
sections.content:
**Kanban** originated in Toyota's manufacturing system in the 1940s as a pull-based scheduling method. David Anderson adapted it for software development in the mid-2000s. Where Scrum organises work into time-boxed iterations, Kanban organises work as a **continuous flow** through defined workflow stages.

The core artefact is the **Kanban board**: columns represent stages of work (To Do → In Progress → In Review → Done), and cards represent individual work items. The board is a live X-ray of the team's system — every piece of in-flight work is visible to everyone, always.

**WIP Limits** are the defining constraint that separates Kanban from a simple task board. Each column has a maximum number of items it can hold simultaneously. When a column is full, no new item may enter it until one flows forward. This creates **pull-based flow**: work is pulled forward by capacity, not pushed by urgency.

Why do WIP limits help? Several reasons:

- **Reduces context switching.** When developers juggle five tasks simultaneously, the cognitive overhead of switching between contexts degrades quality and speed. Limiting WIP forces focus.
- **Surfaces bottlenecks.** If the 'In Review' column is always at its limit while 'In Progress' keeps filling up, the bottleneck is review capacity — you need more reviewers, not more developers.
- **Creates urgency to finish.** When you cannot start new work because WIP is at the limit, you are motivated to unblock the item that is stuck rather than start something new and leave the old item to linger.
- **Reduces cycle time.** **Cycle time** is how long a single item takes from 'started' to 'done'. WIP limit theory (based on **Little's Law**: cycle time = WIP / throughput) predicts that reducing WIP reduces average cycle time — your items finish faster even if you are processing the same amount of work.

**Kanban metrics** are different from Scrum's velocity. Teams track **lead time** (time from request to delivery), **cycle time** (time from start to done), and **throughput** (items completed per week). These metrics feed a **cumulative flow diagram** — a chart that makes queues and flow rates visible over time.

**When to use Kanban vs. Scrum?** Kanban suits work that is continuous and unpredictable: production support queues, bug triages, operations, and maintenance. The demand is irregular, items vary wildly in size, and fitting them into fixed sprints adds overhead without benefit. Scrum suits iterative feature development with predictable planning horizons and team commitment to a Sprint Goal. Many teams use **Scrumban** — a hybrid that keeps Scrum's ceremonies but adds WIP limits and Kanban's flow metrics.

sections.title: Continuous Integration: The Technical Foundation of Fast Delivery
sections.content:
**Continuous Integration (CI)** is the practice of every developer merging their code to the shared main branch at least once per day, with an automated pipeline that builds and tests the code on every push. The term was coined by Grady Booch in 1991 and popularised by Kent Beck as a core Extreme Programming (XP) practice.

The problem CI solves is **integration hell** — the painful experience of developers working in isolation on long-lived branches and then attempting to merge weeks or months of diverged work. The merge conflicts, hidden incompatibilities, and broken assumptions multiply exponentially with the duration of isolation. CI eliminates integration hell by making integration *continuous* — a daily, automated, low-friction act.

**The CI contract has three rules:**

1. Every developer merges to main at least daily.
2. An automated pipeline runs on every push: compile, lint, unit test, integration test.
3. A broken build is the team's **highest priority** — it is fixed before any new work begins.

Rule three is the rule teams most often violate, and its violation undermines the other two. If a broken build is tolerated for hours or days, developers start branching off broken commits, adding their own changes, and you are back to integration hell — just with extra steps.

**CI vs. CD vs. CD (Continuous Delivery vs. Continuous Deployment):** These terms are frequently confused.

- **Continuous Integration (CI)**: Automated build and test on every push. Ensures the main branch is always in a *buildable, tested* state.
- **Continuous Delivery (CD)**: The pipeline goes further — every passing build is automatically prepared for production deployment, but a human gate (button press) triggers the actual release.
- **Continuous Deployment (CD)**: The human gate is removed — every passing build is automatically deployed to production. Requires extremely high test coverage and monitoring confidence.

Most teams operate at Continuous Delivery. Full Continuous Deployment is practiced by organisations like Netflix and Amazon that have invested years in test coverage, feature flags, and canary deployments.

**What does a CI pipeline do?** A well-designed pipeline is structured as sequential gates, each faster than the next:

1. **Install dependencies** — reproducible installs using lockfiles (`npm ci`, not `npm install`)
2. **Lint** — static analysis for code style and obvious bugs (fast, < 1 min)
3. **Unit tests** — isolated, no I/O, fast (< 2 min)
4. **Integration tests** — real database, real services, slower (2–5 min)
5. **E2E tests** — full browser automation, slowest (5–20 min)
6. **Build artefact** — compile, bundle, Docker image
7. **Security scan** — dependency audit, SAST

The fast gates run first. If lint fails, there is no point running E2E tests — the feedback is fast, the wasted time minimal. This principle is called **fail fast**.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
# Runs on every push to main/develop and every pull request
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  # ── Gate 1: Fast feedback (lint + unit tests) ──────────────────
  fast-checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies (reproducible)
        run: npm ci

      - name: Lint (fail fast on style/type errors)
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Unit tests with coverage
        run: npm test -- --coverage --ci

      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          fail_ci_if_error: true

  # ── Gate 2: Slower checks (only after Gate 1 passes) ──────────
  integration-tests:
    needs: fast-checks
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
        ports: ['5432:5432']
        options: --health-cmd pg_isready
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Run migrations against test DB
        run: npm run db:migrate
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:testpass@localhost/test
      - name: Integration tests
        run: npm run test:integration
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:testpass@localhost/test

  # ── Gate 3: E2E — only on PRs targeting main ──────────────────
  e2e:
    needs: integration-tests
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Build app
        run: npm run build:fast
      - name: Playwright E2E tests
        run: npx playwright test
        env:
          BASE_URL: http://localhost:3000
sections.explanation: Three sequential gates implement fail-fast: Gate 1 catches syntax/style/logic errors in under 2 minutes. Gate 2 catches database integration issues. Gate 3 runs full browser tests only on PRs — not on every push to develop, keeping developer feedback fast. The `needs:` keyword creates the dependency chain; a failing gate skips all downstream jobs automatically.

sections.title: Code Review Culture: Peer Feedback as a Team Practice
sections.content:
**Code review** is the practice of having at least one other developer read and critique every code change before it is merged to the main branch. It is one of the most impactful practices a software team can adopt — studies by Capers Jones and others have shown that structured code review is one of the most cost-effective defect detection methods, often catching 60–90% of defects before they reach production.

But catching bugs is only one benefit — arguably not even the most important one:

- **Knowledge sharing**: Reviews spread understanding of every part of the codebase across the team. When Alice reviews Bob's change to the payment module, she learns how that module works. The team accumulates shared context.
- **Collective ownership**: If everyone reviews everything, nobody can say 'I don't touch that code — that's Bob's module.' Everyone is responsible for the whole codebase.
- **Design improvement**: A second pair of eyes often spots simpler approaches, missing abstractions, or design inconsistencies that the original author, too close to the problem, missed.
- **Standards enforcement**: Code style, naming conventions, error handling patterns, and security practices are consistently applied when reviewers actively check for them.

**What makes a good code review?**

As a **reviewer**, the core question is: 'Can I understand what this code does, and does it do it correctly and safely?' Beyond that:
- Does the code do what the PR description claims? (Trust, but verify.)
- Are edge cases handled? (null input, empty arrays, network failure, concurrent access)
- Are there tests for the new behaviour? If not, ask for them.
- Is there duplication that could be extracted? Is there an existing utility this could reuse?
- Are names clear? Good names eliminate the need for comments.
- Are there security concerns? (SQL injection, unvalidated user input, exposed secrets, insecure defaults)
- Does the PR do *one thing*? Large PRs that touch many concerns are hard to review and easy to merge without catching problems.

As an **author**, the mindset shift that makes reviews effective:
- The reviewer's job is to improve your code, not to criticise you.
- Provide context in the PR description: *why* you made this change, *what* you considered and rejected, and *where* reviewers should focus.
- Keep PRs small (ideally under 400 lines of changed code). Small PRs get faster, higher-quality reviews.
- Respond to every comment — either implement the change, or explain why you disagree. Respectful disagreement is fine; silence is not.

**Review culture anti-patterns to avoid:**
- **Rubber-stamp approval**: clicking Approve without reading, just to unblock the merge.
- **Nitpick avalanche**: 40 comments, 35 of which are stylistic preferences the linter should enforce.
- **LGTM with no feedback**: 'Looks good to me' teaches the author nothing and misses issues.
- **Design review in code review**: Fundamental architectural disagreements should be resolved *before* implementation, not after a developer has spent a week building it.
- **Blocking on perfection**: Code review is not the time to demand the perfect solution. 'Good enough to ship, better than before' is a valid outcome.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
## PR: Add Stripe card tokenisation for saved payment methods

### What and Why
Implements US-43 from Sprint 14. Customers currently re-enter card
details on every purchase. This adds tokenisation so cards can be
stored server-side (as Stripe PaymentMethod IDs, never raw numbers)
and reused at checkout without re-entering CVV.

### Changes
- `PaymentService.createPaymentMethod()` — calls Stripe API, stores
  the returned `pm_xxx` token against the user record
- `CheckoutService.chargeWithSavedCard()` — attaches PaymentMethod
  to customer and creates PaymentIntent
- `PaymentController` — two new endpoints: POST /payment-methods,
  POST /checkout/saved-card
- Added `payment_method_id` column to `users` table (migration included)

### What I considered but did not do
- Storing multiple cards per user: out of scope for this sprint;
  the schema uses a single nullable column. Multi-card support is US-47.
- Webhook handling for `payment_intent.payment_failed`: tracked in BUG-12.

### Review focus areas
Please pay extra attention to the Stripe API error handling in
`PaymentService` — I am not certain I have covered all Stripe error
codes. Also check the migration for the nullable column default.

### Testing
- Unit tests: PaymentService (8 tests), CheckoutService (5 tests)
- Integration test: full checkout flow with Stripe test mode
- Manual: tested with Stripe test card 4242 4242 4242 4242

---
## Code Review Checklist (Reviewer)
- [ ] Code matches PR description — no hidden scope
- [ ] Edge cases handled: null card, Stripe API down, duplicate save
- [ ] Tests present for new behaviour (not just happy path)
- [ ] No duplication of existing payment utilities
- [ ] Names are clear without needing comments
- [ ] No secrets or PII in logs or responses
- [ ] Migration is safe to run on production (additive only)
sections.explanation: A good PR description answers: what, why, what was considered and rejected, and where the reviewer should focus. This reduces review time significantly — the reviewer does not have to reverse-engineer the author's intent from the diff alone. The checklist makes review criteria explicit and consistent across all reviewers.

sections.title: How These Practices Reinforce Each Other
sections.content:
Agile practices are not independent choices — they form an **ecosystem** where each practice amplifies the others. Understanding the interactions helps you adopt them strategically rather than cargo-culting the rituals.

**Short sprints require CI.** If a team commits to releasing a working Increment every two weeks, they cannot afford integration hell at the end of the sprint. CI keeps the main branch green continuously, so the end of a sprint is just a normal day — not a frantic merge-and-fix marathon.

**CI requires small, frequent commits.** The 'integrate daily' discipline of CI naturally pushes developers toward smaller, more focused changes. Smaller changes are easier to understand, review, and roll back. This reduces the cognitive load of code review and the blast radius of any single bug.

**Code review requires psychological safety.** The retrospective is the ceremony that builds the psychological safety needed for honest code review. Teams that run good retrospectives — where giving and receiving honest feedback is normal — develop the culture where code review is collaborative rather than adversarial.

**Retrospectives require a stable team.** The compound improvement from retrospectives only accumulates in stable, long-lived teams. This is why Agile's 'self-organising teams' are not just a philosophical preference — they are a structural requirement for the process to work.

**Kanban makes CI bottlenecks visible.** When a Kanban board shows 'In Review' at its WIP limit with items piling up in 'In Progress', the team knows CI reviews are the bottleneck. The board makes systemic problems visible that would be invisible in a backlog-only view.

This ecosystem effect is why Agile transformations that cherry-pick only the ceremonies (standups, sprints) without the technical practices (CI, automated testing, small PRs) rarely achieve the expected results. The practices depend on each other.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Pitfalls
sections.content:
**'Agile means no documentation.'** The Manifesto says working software *over* comprehensive documentation — not *instead of* documentation. A decision log, an architecture decision record (ADR), and a README are not comprehensive documentation — they are the minimal investment that prevents the same mistakes from being made twice. The pathology being rejected was 200-page functional specs that were never updated after month one.

**'Scrum ceremonies are overhead that slows us down.'** Ceremonies feel like overhead when they are run poorly. A 15-minute standup that takes 45 minutes because it has become a status report is genuinely wasteful. But a well-run sprint planning that gives the team a clear shared goal for two weeks is what makes the next two weeks fast. The ceremony is the investment; the focused execution is the return.

**'Story points measure productivity.'** Story points are a **relative complexity estimate** for planning purposes — they answer 'how much can we commit to this sprint?' based on historical velocity. They are not a measure of a developer's productivity, worth, or output. Using story points to compare developers or teams destroys the psychological safety that makes honest estimation possible.

**'The Scrum Master is the team's manager.'** The Scrum Master has no authority over the team. They do not assign tasks, do not evaluate performance, and do not own the plan. They facilitate. Confusing the SM with a project manager is one of the most common Scrum anti-patterns and turns the SM into a micro-manager in process clothing.

**'CI means Continuous Deployment.'** Many teams have CI (automated build and test on every push) without Continuous Delivery or Deployment. CI is the foundation; CD is built on top of it. You can have CI without CD; you cannot safely have CD without CI.

**'Code review is optional for experienced developers.'** The benefits of code review — knowledge sharing, collective ownership, design improvement — apply at every experience level. Senior developers often gain the most from review because their changes touch more critical and complex parts of the system.

sections.content: **A brief history note.** The 17 signatories of the Agile Manifesto included Kent Beck (Extreme Programming), Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland (Scrum), Alistair Cockburn (Crystal), and Martin Fowler (refactoring). Scrum itself was described by Takeuchi and Nonaka in a 1986 Harvard Business Review paper — they used the rugby scrum metaphor for a team moving together as a unit. The Kanban software method was developed by David Anderson at Microsoft and Corbis between 2004 and 2007. CI was formalised by Kent Beck in 'Extreme Programming Explained' (1999) and later popularised by tools like CruiseControl (2001), Hudson (2004), Jenkins (2011), Travis CI (2011), and GitHub Actions (2019).

**Retrospectives are the most underrated Agile ceremony — and the most skipped.** A team that skips retros ships the same problems sprint after sprint. The formula that works: 10 minutes writing sticky notes (what went well / what to improve), 10 minutes grouping and voting, 5 minutes picking ONE actionable improvement with an explicit owner and success criterion, check it at the top of the next retro. One compounding improvement per sprint adds up to a dramatically better team within six months. **Interview insight**: when asked 'how do you improve a team's engineering process?', the answer 'introduce regular retrospectives with one concrete action per cycle' is almost always correct — it shows you understand that process improvement requires deliberate, structured reflection, not just harder work.

items: The **Agile Manifesto** (2001) established four value priorities — individuals, working software, customer collaboration, responding to change — as a reaction to heavyweight waterfall processes that failed under uncertainty.

**Scrum** provides structure through three roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers), five events (Sprint, Planning, Daily Standup, Review, Retrospective), and three artefacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment) — its power is the short feedback loop, not the ceremonies themselves.
**Kanban** controls work flow with WIP limits that surface bottlenecks, reduce context switching, and lower cycle time — it suits continuous, unpredictable work streams better than fixed sprints.

**Continuous Integration** means every developer merges to main daily with an automated build-and-test pipeline; a broken build is the team's top priority — this eliminates integration hell and keeps the main branch always releasable.
**Code review** is about knowledge sharing and collective ownership as much as bug catching — small PRs, clear descriptions, and specific actionable feedback make reviews fast and effective.

The practices **reinforce each other**: short sprints force CI; CI encourages small PRs; small PRs enable fast reviews; retrospectives build the psychological safety for honest feedback — removing any one weakens the whole system.

Common pitfalls: treating story points as productivity metrics, skipping retrospectives, running CI without automated tests, writing large PRs, and adopting Scrum ceremonies without the underlying engineering practices that make them effective.

quiz.question: Which of the following is one of the four value statements in the Agile Manifesto?
options: Comprehensive documentation over working software
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration
Responding to change over following a plan
Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
quiz.explanation: The four Agile values each express a preference: Individuals over processes, Working software over documentation, Customer collaboration over contracts, Responding to change over following a plan. Option C is a direct quote from the Manifesto. The other options invert the stated preferences.

quiz.question: In Scrum, who is solely responsible for ordering the Product Backlog?
options: The Scrum Master
The entire Development Team collectively
The Product Owner
The Engineering Manager
quiz.explanation: The Product Owner owns and orders the Product Backlog, ensuring it reflects the highest-value items first. The Scrum Master facilitates process and removes impediments; the Development Team does the implementation work. There is exactly one PO to avoid conflicting prioritisation signals.

quiz.question: According to Little's Law, what is the relationship between WIP limits and cycle time in a Kanban system?
options: Reducing WIP increases cycle time because fewer items are moving
Reducing WIP reduces average cycle time — items finish faster
WIP limits have no effect on cycle time; they only affect throughput
Cycle time is determined solely by item complexity, not WIP
quiz.explanation: Little's Law states: cycle time = WIP / throughput. For a given throughput (team capacity), reducing WIP directly reduces average cycle time. This is counterintuitive — doing less at once means each thing gets done faster — but it is mathematically proven and empirically observed in software teams.

quiz.question: What is the precise definition of Continuous Integration (CI)?
options: Automatically deploying to production on every passing commit
Running integration tests once per sprint before the Sprint Review
Every developer merges to main at least daily with automated build and tests on every push
A nightly scheduled build job that checks whether the codebase compiles
quiz.explanation: CI has two components: the human practice (frequent integration — at least daily) and the automated practice (build and test pipeline on every push). It is distinct from Continuous Delivery (automated staging/release pipeline) and Continuous Deployment (auto-deploy to production). A nightly build is not CI — it is too infrequent to catch integration conflicts quickly.

quiz.question: The Sprint Retrospective is MOST accurately described as:
options: A demo of completed work shown to stakeholders for product feedback
A planning session where the team selects backlog items for the next sprint
An internal team ceremony to reflect on process and commit to one concrete improvement
A report of sprint velocity and burndown delivered to the Product Owner
quiz.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is an internal team ceremony — no external stakeholders — focused on the team's process, not the product. The output is one actionable improvement owned by someone on the team. The Sprint Review is where stakeholders see the product increment. Sprint Planning selects the next sprint's work.

quiz.question: A CI pipeline is structured with lint first, then unit tests, then integration tests, then E2E tests. Why is this ordering important?
options: E2E tests are most important so they should be saved for last
Faster, cheaper checks run first so failures give immediate feedback without running slow, expensive tests
Lint must complete before the compiler can process the code
This order is a GitHub Actions requirement, not a design choice
quiz.explanation: The 'fail fast' principle: if lint catches a syntax error in 30 seconds, there is no reason to spend 15 minutes on E2E tests that will also fail. Running fast gates first minimises wasted CI minutes and gives developers immediate, targeted feedback. The order is a deliberate design choice, not a tool requirement.

quiz.question: What does 'collective code ownership' mean in Agile engineering culture?
options: All code changes must be approved by the tech lead who owns the module
Any team member can improve any part of the codebase; no single person owns a file
All developers are assigned specific modules they alone are responsible for maintaining
The original author must review and approve all future changes to their code
quiz.explanation: Collective ownership means anyone on the team can and should improve any part of the codebase. This removes knowledge silos, prevents single points of failure ('only Alice understands the payment module'), and is how code review actively spreads knowledge across the team. It requires psychological safety — enabled by good retrospective culture.

quiz.question: A developer has been working on a feature branch for 3 weeks without merging. According to CI best practices, what is the PRIMARY risk?
options: The feature branch will be deleted automatically after 2 weeks
Integration hell: the long divergence makes merging back to main painful and conflict-prone
The CI pipeline will refuse to run on branches older than 2 weeks
Other developers cannot see the work, reducing collaboration opportunities
quiz.explanation: Long-lived feature branches accumulate divergence from main. When they eventually merge, the conflicts, incompatibilities, and hidden assumptions that accumulated over 3 weeks must all be resolved at once — this is 'integration hell'. CI's core discipline of daily integration is specifically designed to prevent this by keeping divergence to at most 24 hours.

quiz.question: Which situation is Kanban generally BETTER suited to than Scrum?
options: A team building a major new feature over 3 months with clear Sprint Goals
A team doing production support, bug fixes, and ops where demand is continuous and unpredictable
A team that needs explicit roles (PO, SM) to manage stakeholder expectations
A team releasing a planned new feature on a fixed two-week schedule
quiz.explanation: Kanban suits continuous flow work — production support queues, operations, maintenance — where demand is irregular and items vary wildly in size. Fitting these into fixed sprints adds ceremony overhead without benefit. Scrum's cadence and Sprint Goal structure works better for iterative feature development with predictable demand.

quiz.question: A CI build breaks on the main branch. According to CI best practices, what should happen next?
options: The developer who broke it should immediately revert their commit regardless of the cause
The team should temporarily disable the failing test until the next sprint
Fixing the build becomes the team's highest priority — no new work starts until main is green
The CI system should automatically retry three times before notifying anyone
quiz.explanation: A broken main branch blocks every developer who needs to integrate their work. CI's core discipline: fix it immediately, with team help if needed. Disabling tests or retrying without investigation destroys the CI contract. Reverting may be appropriate if the fix will take hours, but the goal is always a green main branch as fast as possible.
